idea: Many useful systems face the same ordinary problem: something has already happened, and the next choice depends on the order of those earlier events. A student asks questions over many sessions, a driver moves through a city, a viewer watches short videos, a battery load rises and falls, and none of these records is just a bag of unrelated facts. The first event changes the meaning of the second, and the second changes what the third can sensibly be. A simple count of what happened most often loses this ordering, so it cannot tell whether a user is settling into a stable habit, drifting toward a new topic, or reacting to one recent event. Predicting a sequence means keeping a compact memory of the past that is useful for the next step. The memory may be the last minute of power readings, a chain of locations and times, a dialogue history split at topic changes, or a user's long and short news interests. The question is always: which pieces of the past still matter now, and which are old noise? The answer cannot be a fixed rule, because different streams forget at different speeds. Short-video interest can turn quickly, programming knowledge may build more slowly, and traffic may depend on several recent time scales at once. Sequence modeling is the disciplined way to learn those different rhythms from ordered examples and turn them into a next guess.
why: The idea works when the near future is partly constrained by the path that led to the present. If many users watch one kind of video and then soon watch another, that ordered pair carries more evidence than either video alone. If a city's traffic sensors show the same morning build-up across many days, the last few readings make some next readings more likely than others. The useful promise is not certainty; it is a better guess after conditioning on history, meaning the estimate changes once the recent past is known. This breaks when the past is weak evidence, when the world changes faster than the model can relearn, or when the record hides the event that truly caused the next step. More context can also hurt, as the time-interval prediction paper asks, because old details may distract from the small part of history that actually controls the next purchase time. The strongest sequence systems therefore learn both remembering and forgetting. They keep enough history to catch long patterns, but they must also decide when a fresh signal should outweigh a stale one.
math: The mathematical object is an ordered record plus a rule for updating belief after each new event. At every step, the system has a current summary of the past, sees one more item, time gap, word, location, rating, comment, or sensor reading, and revises what it thinks may happen next. Probability enters as plain bookkeeping for uncertainty: instead of saying one future must happen, the system gives larger weight to futures that have often followed similar histories. Comparison also matters, because the system must decide whether two histories are similar enough that evidence from one should help with the other. In recommendation, the output is often a ranked list, so the math turns a changing user history into scores for candidate videos, articles, or products. In forecasting, the output is a future value or time interval, so the math measures how wrong past forecasts were and adjusts the rule to reduce that error. In memory systems, the hard move is compression: saving only the parts of a long conversation or document stream that may be needed later. In event modeling, time gaps are part of the evidence, because two events close together can mean something different from the same two events months apart. The central tradeoff is memory versus noise: hold too little and the system misses long causes; hold too much and old or irrelevant events blur the signal. The principle fits these papers because their data is not only about what occurred, but about the order, spacing, and changing force of what occurred.
family: These papers are siblings because they all refuse to treat a record as a flat pile. Their shared problem shape is a stream whose meaning changes as it unfolds: clicks, purchases, locations, comments, power readings, search queries, meeting words, radio-map layers, or molecule-building steps. The repeated failure mode is a method that either remembers only the latest event or remembers everything with equal force. Remembering only the latest event misses slow preference, learning, risk, and traffic patterns. Remembering everything equally wastes time and can let old behavior drown out the present. The common mathematical move is to carry forward a summary of the past, update it when a new event arrives, and use that summary to score the next likely step. What changed in this group is the pressure to do this across longer histories, larger industrial logs, mixed signals, and real-time settings where slow exhaustive reading is too expensive. The papers differ in surface task, but they share the same need to decide what the past is still saying now.
dots: VK-LSVD makes the family concrete at industrial scale: billions of short-video interactions are useful because the order of watching, skipping, liking, and sharing reveals fast interest shifts. SEAR, Token-level Collaborative Alignment, and the reasoning-based recommendation paper all ask how past user choices should guide the next recommendation, while adding item meaning, ratings, or written reasons so the sequence is not just a bare click trail. ONeRec and the stage-wise news paper focus on drift, where a user has both stable interests and a recent direction of movement. GenCI makes the same point for clicks by separating longer preference from immediate intent before scoring candidates. HingeMem and ES-MemEval move the idea into conversation: a support or dialogue system must remember scattered disclosures, changing topics, and conflicts across sessions without treating every old sentence as equally relevant. TRACE and the spatio-temporal intelligence paper use location sequences, where missing or future movement can be inferred only if the path and timing are respected. The 12V power-load study, MIGC-CMamba, Time-TK, RadioAR, and the web-scale forecasting optimizer all treat sensor or signal history as evidence for future load, traffic, time-series values, or radio strength. Mamba Hawkes Process and the arbitrage paper emphasize irregular events, where both the event type and the time gap change what the next event should mean. Probe-and-Fetch applies the same family logic to long-document use: predict which earlier parts will matter soon, then fetch those instead of carrying everything. The molecule generation and trajectory recovery papers show the constructive version of the idea, where the system creates or repairs an object step by step while each new step must remain consistent with the partial sequence already built.
picture: Imagine a cook tasting soup while it simmers. The next action depends on the order of what already happened: salt before boiling is not the same as salt after reduction, and one recent taste may matter more than an old note in the recipe. Sequence prediction is that habit turned into a rule: keep the parts of the history that still change the next move, ignore what no longer helps, and act one step at a time.
